item.title: AI-Built Torrent Site Looks Inside Downloads to Catch Fakes and Malware
item.description:
Home > AI >

In recent years, AI has made it much easier to create new websites and tools. That also applies to pirate sites, including TorrentClaw, a torrent search engine that’s largely built with AI. The site's TrueSpec feature, for example, checks what’s inside torrents. The results reveal a recurring malware trick, where a genuine VLC player is used as a decoy to load a malicious file.

TorrentClaw is a relatively new torrent search engine that launched in February.

The site is built on links from its own DHT crawler and dozens of external torrent sites and aggregators. In just a few months, the site has grown into an index of more than six million torrents, including the latest Hollywood blockbusters and hit series.

The homepage looks more modern than traditional torrent sites and has some clear AI-design tells. That’s not a secret. On the contrary, AI plays a central role in the site’s development and marketing.

TorrentClaw.com

According to TorrentClaw’s developers, who all use the name Deivid Soto, the platform is largely built and run with the help of AI.

“Basically, the core framework is Claude Code combined with local LLMs for specific execution and ingestion tasks,” Soto tells us.

For example, AI is used to match torrents to film and TV titles, so these can be neatly organized. The AI-driven categorization process takes over tasks that would otherwise be manual work, and AI helped to build novel tools as well.

One of the features built this way is TrueSpec, which checks whether torrents actually contain what their names suggest. That helps to spot fake torrents and malware.

TrueSpec: Download and Verify

On most torrent sites, release names are the main source of information for torrent users. They list the resolution, codec, audio and release group, but there’s no guarantee that any of it is accurate.

Mislabeled torrents are often handled by moderators on well-run torrent sites, but most automated indexes have no active moderation. That’s where TrueSpec comes in.

TrueSpec joins the torrent swarm, reads the file listing, and downloads enough pieces to check the video with the analysis tool ffprobe. According to the site and its developers, that’s between 10 and 20 MB per torrent.

TrueSpec

In addition to verifying the names, TrueSpec also checks suspicious files. It looks up their hashes on VirusTotal and, if the files are small enough, uploads these for a scan. TorrentClaw doesn’t run its own virus scanner, the malware verdicts come from VirusTotal.

When TrueSpec finds malware, the torrent remains listed on the site, but with a “Malware detected” label and the download button disabled. At the time of writing, one fake Jujutsu Kaisen episode with this label still had 34 seeders while it remained available on some external sites.

‘Malware detected’

Not Perfect

The TrueSpec system isn’t perfect. In July, an earlier dataset counted 6,450 malware cases, but many were false positives. These included the harmless RARBG_DO_NOT_MIRROR.exe file, fansub scripts that switch audio languages, and scripts that simply open a website.

The TrueSpec data from late September paints a different picture. TorrentClaw now only counts malware when VirusTotal confirms it, which leaves 34 torrents. We checked some of these against the evidence in the data, which links to a VirusTotal report for every confirmed case.

Detected malware is rare, but the count is likely too low. TrueSpec doesn’t download large executables, it prioritizes well-seeded torrents, and dead swarms can’t be checked at all. TorrentClaw also focuses on films and TV shows, so pirated software and games are largely left out.

Malware is only part of what TrueSpec flags. In total, 1,265 of the 687,057 probed torrents were flagged as deceptive, including programs disguised as videos and fake resolutions. That’s less than 0.2% of all checked torrents.

The most common type of ‘mislabeling’ is actually quite harmless. More than half of all probed torrents, 55%, include subtitle tracks that their release names don’t mention. TorrentClaw flags this as a missing label, but subtitles are typically not added to titles unless they are hardcoded. Scene rules don’t require this either.

VLC Player Malware

Most of the confirmed malware torrents follow the same pattern. In 31 of the 34 cases, the torrent includes an executable named after a new episode or film, a file called libvlc.dll, and a playable video in a subfolder.

The application is a renamed copy of the genuine VLC media player. According to TorrentClaw, it’s identical to VideoLAN’s official release and carries its code signature. The malicious part is the DLL, which VLC loads when it starts, and which VirusTotal engines flag as a trojan.

The torrents are named after popular new releases, including episodes of The Boys, Jujutsu Kaisen and Frieren, and films such as Dune: Part Three and Zootopia 2. Many also carry the names of known release or distribution groups, including SubsPlease, ETHEL and YTS.

This type of malware vector is not new. Earlier this year, a security researcher documented a campaign that used fake SubsPlease releases on Nyaa to spread the Vidar infostealer. These were reportedly uploaded from a stolen account.

TorrentClaw sourced its 31 torrents between February and August. Most of them, 22, came in through its own DHT crawler, while the rest were found via Nyaa, The Pirate Bay and TorrentDownload. All had seeders when indexed, and 15 were still active in early October, according to Soto.

Built For AI, By AI

TrueSpec isn’t the only thing that sets TorrentClaw apart. The torrent site also offers an MCP server, which allows AI assistants such as Claude and Cursor to search the index and fetch .torrent files directly.

MCP server

Technically, this means that users can ask an AI assistant to find a release and load the torrent file, without ever visiting the site. According to Soto, some accounts make around 10,000 API requests a day, which might be external sites or services that use it.

Running TrueSpec doesn’t cost much either. In July, Soto said the system ran on three nodes costing well under $50 a month combined.

“The implicit point: if verification is this cheap, any indexer could be doing it, and none are,” Soto explained.

That said, partially downloading content from hundreds of thousands of torrents can also come with a legal cost. TorrentClaw’s DMCA page states that the site doesn’t host, store, upload or distribute files, but rightsholders may see things differently.

When asked about this, Soto describes TrueSpec as a read-only client that doesn’t upload or seed. It only fetches the first part of a video file, enough to read the container headers.

“[It] deletes everything once the analysis is done. We don’t store or serve any content, and we process every valid takedown notice we receive,” Soto says.

TorrentClaw also uses AI to handle these notices. It introduced an AI-managed system in late September that has handled 23 takedowns so far. Before that, the site received just over 300 notices, mostly duplicates.

TorrentClaw also charges for its premium features. PRO costs $3.99 a month, while PRO+ adds a VPN for $6.99. Whether that business model will hold up has yet to be seen, but commercial torrent services typically draw more attention from rightsholders than free ones.

item.title: Game Industry Asks U.S. to Flag Denuvo Cracker ‘voices38’ as Notorious Piracy Threat
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

The Entertainment Software Association has asked the U.S. Government to label the Denuvo cracker ‘voices38’ as a notorious piracy market. The game industry group argues that the cracker is an essential source in the game piracy ecosystem, feeding repackers and torrent sites. A notorious market flag is no guarantee of success, however, as FitGirl's previous listings show.

Every year, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) asks rightsholders to nominate the foreign piracy sites and services they see as the biggest threats.

The resulting list of ‘notorious markets‘ traditionally features torrent sites, cyberlockers and streaming portals. In recent years, hosting companies and other intermediaries were added as well.

Last week, the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which represents many of the major video game companies, submitted its latest recommendations. These include the usual suspects, but also a target that doesn’t have a website of its own.

A Game Cracker as a Piracy ‘Market’

ESA’s submission lists ‘voices38’ as one of its new threats. The game industry group describes the anonymous cracker as a persistent operation that specializes in beating Denuvo Anti-Tamper, the popular technical protection measure that’s used by at least nine of its members.

Voices38

According to ESA, Reddit’s r/CrackWatch index attributes roughly two dozen cracked or bypassed games to ‘voices38’. The gaming group stresses that the cracker plays a key role in the piracy ecosystem as its releases are picked up by repackers, torrent sites, cyberlockers and piracy forums.

“Each crack therefore unlocks an entire downstream market for an unauthorized copy of that title. For a title that no other actor has made usable, but for Voices38’s crack there would be no functioning pirated copy for those markets to offer,” the submission notes.

“Treating only those downstream services as markets would overlook the upstream operation that determines whether protected games can be offered by them at all.”

The fact that the cracker has no public identity or “traditional homepage” shouldn’t stand in the way of a Notorious Markets listing either, ESA notes. In fact, it argues that a listing could help rightsholders crack down on the cracking operation.

“Designation would focus attention on identifying the operator, preserving evidence, disrupting distribution accounts and donation channels, and coordinating action across the forums, repositories, hosting services, peer-to-peer infrastructure, and other intermediaries used to seed each release,” ESA writes.

ESA’s recommendation

Ideally, ESA would like to identify the person or people behind the popular cracker handle and it’s not alone in this. Identifying the operator is also what Denuvo is trying to do through a U.S. federal court.

Lawsuit Doesn’t Stop the Cracks

Last month, Denuvo sued ‘voices38’ at a California federal court and it recently asked for permission to subpoena Discord, Valve and Reddit. ESA’s submission doesn’t mention this lawsuit.

So far, this hasn’t stopped the cracks from coming out. After a few quiet weeks, ‘voices38’ released cracks for Atomfall and The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales last week, as well as a crackfix for Dead Space Remake.

Atomfall-voices38

These releases swiftly spread over torrent sites and cyberlockers. Popular repacker FitGirl has already picked them up too, which brings us to ESA’s next target.

Billion Dollar FitGirl

After already being included in USTR’s 2024 and 2025 notorious markets lists, FitGirl gets a recommendation from ESA for the next installment.

FitGirl’s site is currently blocked in Germany, Italy, Spain and elsewhere, but ESA notes that these measures didn’t change much. The repack site received 41.77 million visits in August and continues to offer games published by ESA members.

“FitGirl’s scale and persistence demonstrate that prior blocking and designation have not induced meaningful remediation by its operator. ESA’s takedown notices to the site are ignored, with zero links removed between August 2025 and August 2026,” ESA writes.

The game companies also put a billion-dollar price tag on the losses, which they report down to the last cent.

“Between March and August 2026 alone, ESA detected 15,484,145 users in peer-to-peer swarms for games repacked by FitGirl, with an estimated lost value of $1,083,735,308.55,” the submission notes.

A footnote explains that this figure is based on a retail price of $69.99 for every user ESA spotted in a swarm.

Hypothetical Losses

Other targets are not very responsive either. DODI-Repacks removed 22% of the reported links and RuTracker, the Russian torrent site, complied with just 3% of ESA’s notices over the past year.

While these sites are not responding, ESA highlights that tracking their finances, including crypto transactions that go to KYC-vetted platforms such as Binance, could help to identify these targets.

Handheld Consoles as ‘Superfakes’

This year, the USTR’s review has a special focus on high-quality counterfeit goods, known as superfakes. ESA uses this opportunity to highlight handheld consoles that come preloaded with pirated games, which it sees as the video game equivalent of superfakes.

The group nominates Anbernic.com, the official store for a widely sold line of handheld emulation devices. ESA says these are routinely offered or shipped with memory cards that hold hundreds or thousands of unauthorized games, and notes that they are sold through Amazon and eBay as well.

The submission further lists G2A, FunPay and Eldorado.gg, where game accounts and in-game items are traded, as well as cheat sellers including Cronus Zen. ESA argues that cheats belong on a piracy list because they circumvent the technological protection measures of games.

It’s now up to the USTR to decide which of these recommendations make the final list. The previous edition was published in March, so we might have to wait a while before the final Notorious Markets list arrives.

—

A copy of ESA’s submission for the 2026 Notorious Markets review is available here (pdf).

item.title: MPA Takes Credit for Shutting Down Piracy Giants AnimeFLV and Cineby
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

When pirate streaming giant Cineby shut down at the end of August, its operators blamed the loss of their main video providers. Now, the MPA informs the U.S. Trade Representative that the site stopped operating following "MPA and ACE actions," adding that the same applies to anime piracy portal AnimeFLV. At the same time, the MPA flags several persistent piracy threats, including Telegram, Kisskh, and MagisTV.

With more than 160 million visits in July, Cineby was one of the most popular pirate streaming sites on the Internet.

That changed in August, when the operators announced a surprise shutdown. The site was taken offline in stages over more than a week, with the last domains going dark in early September.

At first, the operators did not explain why they threw in the towel. In a final statement, however, they said that their two main video providers, which they named as the “Sflix group” and “1Movies group,” went down about three months earlier, and that the service never fully recovered.

No anti-piracy operation was mentioned and the usual enforcement groups, including the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE), did not claim it either, until now.

The MPA Takes Credit

Last week, the Motion Picture Association (MPA) sent its annual overview of notorious foreign piracy markets to the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR). Before listing the threats that remain, the Hollywood group highlights what it sees as positive developments since its previous submission.

The demise of Cineby is one of them, together with the linked embed service Videasy.

“On another positive note, 2025 submissions Cineby[.]app and Videasy[.]net have ceased operations following MPA and ACE actions,” the MPA writes.

MPA and ACE actions

Earlier in the new filing, the MPA links the takedown of Cineby-associated domains to an “extensive investigation and multi-region enforcement effort.”

Following this effort, the main cineby.at domain is “nonfunctional” and Videasy is offline, the MPA notes. Vidking, which is mentioned alongside them, is still accessible but “has no connected source servers.”

The submission doesn’t mention a court or a police force, so it appears to be a private enforcement effort. Further details are not shared.

The same filing does credit Vietnamese law enforcement with dismantling the HiAnime piracy network, which according to the MPA also included Sflix/MyFlixer and Megacloud/Vidcloud. Seven suspected operators were charged in July.

This is likely the same “Sflix group” Cineby referred to, suggesting that Cineby used services from the Vietnamese group that was shut down.

While the MPA lists Cineby as “no longer active,” the brand hasn’t disappeared entirely. There are several copycats that popped up, including cineby.vg, which the MPA mentions in its report.

AnimeFLV Too

Cineby isn’t the only unexplained shutdown that the MPA now counts as a victory. The submission also lists the Spanish-language anime portal AnimeFLV, which previously received more than a billion annual visits, according to the MPA.

“Additionally, the AnimeFLV family of sites included in last year’s submission has shut down following MPA and ACE actions. This shutdown represents a significant enforcement success,” the MPA writes.

AnimeFLV

In July, we reported that AnimeFLV had stopped serving video in mid-June. The operators stayed silent and no anti-piracy group took credit, until now.

Today, the AnimeFLV domain no longer loads anything. Instead, it returns an HTTP 502 error. Of course, this brand has also been taken over by copycats since.

The Hydra Keeps Growing

Aside from the successes, the MPA’s submission lists dozens of sites and services that remain a problem. The group stresses that its overview is not intended to be comprehensive, but it highlights several key threats.

Last year, Myflixerz/Sflix, Cuevana, and HiAnime were listed as priority linking and streaming sites. This year, Kisskh is the only priority entry, while Cuevana moved to the regular list.

Kisskh, which specializes in Asian dramas and Hollywood content, received more than 70 million visits on its kisskh.is domain in August, mostly from India.

The “hydra sites” category that the MPA introduced last year remains a key concern. These pirate portals often rely on third-party Piracy-as-a-Service (PaaS) platforms for their videos. This includes the live sports PaaS service Streamed.

According to the MPA, the roughly 30 sites that use the live sports PaaS Streamed had 463 million visits in July, up from 134 million a year earlier.

New hydra threats include 1Shows/1Flex, CineHD/VidBox, and StreamEX. On the PaaS side, Videasy and MegaCloud are shut down and no longer listed, but there are newcomers. VidFast, for example, is reportedly used by at least 158 pirate sites with roughly 629 million monthly visits combined.

In the cyberlockers and video hosting category, Telegram now tops the priority list, while DoodStream moved to the regular list. Among other things, the MPA notes that Telegram’s response to takedown notices ranges from swift processing to weeks of inaction.

“Telegram is a platform of immediate concern,” the MPA writes.

Immediate concern

In the hosting category, the MPA shares new details on Netulu, which was already mentioned last year. The company was incorporated in Delaware in April and MPA says that, at that time, all piracy sites hosted by Private Layer were transferred to it. According to the MPA, U.S.-based investigators are “following leads.”

Following leads

Pirate app MovieBox is back on the list as well. The MPA cites more than 243 million downloads from Palm Store alone, but as we reported last week, the store’s counter has already passed 300 million.

The USTR will review the MPA’s submission, together with input from other stakeholders, in the coming months. Its own notorious markets list is expected early next year.

—

A list of all sites and services highlighted and categorized in the MPA’s 2026 notorious markets submission (pdf) can be found below. For additional context, we highlight the new entries, while also indicating those from the 2025 report that have since been removed.

Linking and Streaming Websites

Priority sites

– Kisskh.is / Kisskh.do / Kisskh.co (previously additional)
– Myflixerz / Sflix
– Hianime.to, hianime.nz, etc

Additional sites

– 1Shows / 1Flex (new)
– 1tamilmv
– Animeflv.net
– Anime-Sama.to
– Animepahe.ru (new)
– Aniwaves.ru (new)
– Buffstream.io
– Burningseries.ac (bs.to)
– Cda.pl
– Cineby.app
– CineHD / VidBox (new)
– Cuevana3i.bio (previously priority)
– Dytt8899.com, dytt8.net, dytt89.com, etc.
– Gimy.ai
– Goojara.to / levidia.ch / supernova.to
– HydraHD.ru / HydraHD.ws
– Librefutboltv.su

When pirate streaming giant Cineby shut down at the end of August, its operators blamed the loss of their main video providers. Now, the MPA informs the U.S. Trade Representative that the site stopped operating following "MPA and ACE actions," adding that the same applies to anime piracy portal AnimeFLV. At the same time, the MPA flags several persistent piracy threats, including Telegram, Kisskh, and MagisTV.

With more than 160 million visits in July, Cineby was one of the most popular pirate streaming sites on the Internet.

That changed in August, when the operators announced a surprise shutdown. The site was taken offline in stages over more than a week, with the last domains going dark in early September.

At first, the operators did not explain why they threw in the towel. In a final statement, however, they said that their two main video providers, which they named as the “Sflix group” and “1Movies group,” went down about three months earlier, and that the service never fully recovered.

No anti-piracy operation was mentioned and the usual enforcement groups, including the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE), did not claim it either, until now.

The MPA Takes Credit

Last week, the Motion Picture Association (MPA) sent its annual overview of notorious foreign piracy markets to the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR). Before listing the threats that remain, the Hollywood group highlights what it sees as positive developments since its previous submission.

The demise of Cineby is one of them, together with the linked embed service Videasy.

“On another positive note, 2025 submissions Cineby[.]app and Videasy[.]net have ceased operations following MPA and ACE actions,” the MPA writes.

MPA and ACE actions

Earlier in the new filing, the MPA links the takedown of Cineby-associated domains to an “extensive investigation and multi-region enforcement effort.”

Following this effort, the main cineby.at domain is “nonfunctional” and Videasy is offline, the MPA notes. Vidking, which is mentioned alongside them, is still accessible but “has no connected source servers.”

The submission doesn’t mention a court or a police force, so it appears to be a private enforcement effort. Further details are not shared.

The same filing does credit Vietnamese law enforcement with dismantling the HiAnime piracy network, which according to the MPA also included Sflix/MyFlixer and Megacloud/Vidcloud. Seven suspected operators were charged in July.

This is likely the same “Sflix group” Cineby referred to, suggesting that Cineby used services from the Vietnamese group that was shut down.

While the MPA lists Cineby as “no longer active,” the brand hasn’t disappeared entirely. There are several copycats that popped up, including cineby.vg, which the MPA mentions in its report.

AnimeFLV Too

Cineby isn’t the only unexplained shutdown that the MPA now counts as a victory. The submission also lists the Spanish-language anime portal AnimeFLV, which previously received more than a billion annual visits, according to the MPA.

“Additionally, the AnimeFLV family of sites included in last year’s submission has shut down following MPA and ACE actions. This shutdown represents a significant enforcement success,” the MPA writes.

AnimeFLV

In July, we reported that AnimeFLV had stopped serving video in mid-June. The operators stayed silent and no anti-piracy group took credit, until now.

Today, the AnimeFLV domain no longer loads anything. Instead, it returns an HTTP 502 error. Of course, this brand has also been taken over by copycats since.

The Hydra Keeps Growing

Aside from the successes, the MPA’s submission lists dozens of sites and services that remain a problem. The group stresses that its overview is not intended to be comprehensive, but it highlights several key threats.

Last year, Myflixerz/Sflix, Cuevana, and HiAnime were listed as priority linking and streaming sites. This year, Kisskh is the only priority entry, while Cuevana moved to the regular list.

Kisskh, which specializes in Asian dramas and Hollywood content, received more than 70 million visits on its kisskh.is domain in August, mostly from India.

The “hydra sites” category that the MPA introduced last year remains a key concern. These pirate portals often rely on third-party Piracy-as-a-Service (PaaS) platforms for their videos. This includes the live sports PaaS service Streamed.

According to the MPA, the roughly 30 sites that use the live sports PaaS Streamed had 463 million visits in July, up from 134 million a year earlier.

New hydra threats include 1Shows/1Flex, CineHD/VidBox, and StreamEX. On the PaaS side, Videasy and MegaCloud are shut down and no longer listed, but there are newcomers. VidFast, for example, is reportedly used by at least 158 pirate sites with roughly 629 million monthly visits combined.

In the cyberlockers and video hosting category, Telegram now tops the priority list, while DoodStream moved to the regular list. Among other things, the MPA notes that Telegram’s response to takedown notices ranges from swift processing to weeks of inaction.

“Telegram is a platform of immediate concern,” the MPA writes.

Immediate concern

In the hosting category, the MPA shares new details on Netulu, which was already mentioned last year. The company was incorporated in Delaware in April and MPA says that, at that time, all piracy sites hosted by Private Layer were transferred to it. Following leads

Pirate app MovieBox is back on the list as well. The MPA cites more than 243 million downloads from Palm Store alone, but as we reported last week, the store’s counter has already passed 300 million.

item.title: Publishers Seek $19.5m From Pirate Library WeLib, Recycle Anna’s Archive Claims
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

A group of major publishers has asked a New York federal court to issue a $19.5 million default judgment against pirate library WeLib. The site allegedly copied its code and most of its collection from Anna's Archive, which lost a nearly identical case in May. Ironically, the publishers' brief appears to 'copy' from Anna's Archive as well, or at least from their own lawsuit against the shadow library.

Last year, Anna’s Archive warned its users about WeLib, a “new entrant” in the shadow library ecosystem.

The site appeared to have mirrored most of Anna’s collection and used a fork of its codebase. Since WeLib wasn’t sharing new collections or code improvements in return, Anna’s Archive cautioned prospective users.

“We recommend not using them,” the team wrote at the time.

In June, major book publishers came to a similar conclusion, but for different reasons. They filed a lawsuit against WeLib in New York federal court, alleging that the site “was created after its operators copied the source code and most of the contents of” Anna’s Archive.

WeLib

Despite these and other copyright infringement allegations, WeLib’s anonymous operators never responded to the lawsuit. This prompted the publishers to move forward and the court clerk entered a default in August, opening the door to a final judgment request.

$19.5 Million, Again

On Monday, the publishers, including Penguin Random House, Elsevier, and HarperCollins, asked U.S. District Judge Victor Marrero to issue a default judgment against WeLib and its unnamed operators.

“Defendant WeLib is a pirate site whose sole business is the distribution of protected content in violation of the rights of Plaintiffs and other copyright owners,” their brief reads.

The publishers request the maximum statutory damages of $150,000 for each of the 130 works listed in the complaint, ten per publisher. That adds up to $19.5 million, the same amount Judge Jed Rakoff awarded in the Anna’s Archive case.

Damages calculation

Plaintiff Amount
Apress Media, LLC $1,500,000
Cengage Learning, Inc. $1,500,000
Elsevier Inc. $1,500,000
Hachette Book Group, Inc. $1,500,000
HarperCollins Publishers LLC $1,500,000
John Wiley & Sons, Inc. $1,500,000
Macmillan Learning $1,500,000
Macmillan Publishing Group, LLC $1,500,000
McGraw Hill LLC $1,500,000
Pearson Education, Inc. $1,500,000
Penguin Random House LLC $1,500,000
Simon and Schuster, LLC $1,500,000
Taylor & Francis Group LLC $1,500,000
Total: $19,500,000

The brief also puts a spotlight on WeLib’s revenue model. The site can be used for free, but it asks users for “donations” of up to $90 a month. According to the publishers, these are simply payments for faster downloads.

In addition to the damages, the publishers want a permanent injunction. This would require domain registries and registrars to disable welib.org, welib.st, and welib-public.org, and to block their transfer to anyone other than the publishers. Hosting providers would have to stop serving the sites.

Named intermediaries

The injunction would apply to all applicable intermediaries, but the proposed order names five specifically: Public Interest Registry, Cloudflare, Tucows, and two Njalla entities. That’s a much shorter list than the Anna’s Archive judgment, which named more than twenty.

Borrowed From Anna’s Archive

It is not unusual that arguments from a similar case are reused and that also applies here. Large parts of the WeLib brief mirror the one that law firm Oppenheim + Zebrak filed against Anna’s Archive in May, on behalf of the same publishers.

However, not everything fits. According to the brief, WeLib diverts revenue from the publishers “at a scale made worse by their use of the viral BitTorrent protocol.”

We haven’t seen any evidence that WeLib uses BitTorrent, and the WeLib complaint doesn’t mention it either. Instead, the cited paragraphs discuss various harms including lost sales and harm to the market for AI training data.

The same sentence appears, word for word, in the brief against Anna’s Archive. There, it was backed up by the complaint, which described how Anna’s Archive offers torrent files for bulk downloads on a dedicated “Torrents” page.

Same sentence, different site

WeLib’s own complaint mentions another download mechanism. It describes how the site serves files directly from its servers, through “slow” and paid “fast” downloads.

The brief also mentions that WeLib’s infringement continued “despite this and several other cases against them.” That entire paragraph comes straight from the Anna’s Archive brief. While Anna’s Archive was sued before, we are not aware of any other lawsuits against WeLib’s operators.

Even a typo and a garbled sentence with a double negative were copied. Both briefs mention what happens if the court “is satified” that the default standards are met, and both argue that the defendants “cannot establish that they have not presented any meritorious defenses.”

A Paper Victory?

It’s now up to Judge Marrero to decide on the request. Whatever the outcome, the publishers are unlikely to collect much, if anything, as WeLib’s operators remain anonymous.

Anna’s Archive lost several domains to an earlier injunction obtained by music companies. However, it remains online through .gl, .pk, and .gd domains, which are tied to registries and registrars outside the United States.

If Anna’s Archive is any indication, the injunction may cost WeLib some of its domains. However, that is no guarantee that the site will shut down permanently.

—

A copy of the publishers’ memorandum in support of the motion for default judgment is available here (pdf). The proposed default judgment and the statement of damages can be found here (pdf) and here (pdf). The publishers’ earlier brief against Anna’s Archive is available here (pdf).

We reached out to Oppenheim + Zebrak for comment on the BitTorrent claim, but they did not respond before publication.

item.title: RIAA Flags Anna’s Archive and AI Voice Cloner to U.S. Government
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

The RIAA has submitted its latest overview of "notorious markets" to the U.S. Government. It lists familiar names such as The Pirate Bay and Rapidgator, but the music group also flags shadow library Anna's Archive and AI voice-cloning service Lalals. The RIAA presents both as "additional" areas of concern, not as official watchlist candidates.

Every year, the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) invites rightsholders and other stakeholders to suggest foreign sites and services for its list of “notorious markets.”

The annual review doesn’t make any legal findings. Instead, it aims to encourage the listed services, and the countries they operate from, to take proper action against piracy and counterfeiting.

Last week, the RIAA responded with a submission that mostly mentions familiar targets. It lists torrent sites, stream-rippers and cyberlockers, many of which were flagged in previous years. There are some notable newcomers too, including Anna’s Archive.

Anna’s Archive and the Spotify Scrape

In December last year, the shadow library announced that it had downloaded 86 million music files from Spotify, plus metadata for 256 million tracks. This prompted an aggressive legal response.

A few days later, the RIAA coordinated an emergency court action on behalf of its members and Spotify, which resulted in a temporary restraining order against the site. Following this order, domain registry PIR suspended the site’s .org domain, and RIAA says Cloudflare also stopped providing services to the shadow library.

Following this crackdown, Anna’s Archive initially reported that its Spotify metadata torrent was “unavailable until further notice.” In February, however, the site quietly released roughly 3 million music files.

While the torrents for those releases were delisted shortly after, the lawsuit continued, with the labels and Spotify on the winning end.

“On April 14, 2026, RIAA and Spotify obtained a $322 million default judgment against the unknown operators of Anna’s Archive,” the RIAA writes in its USTR submission.

From RIAA’s submission

Despite the legal victory, the music group stresses that Anna’s Archive remains available through its .gl, .pk and .gd domains.

The RIAA isn’t the only rightsholder group that flagged the shadow library to the USTR. The Association of American Publishers (AAP) also lists Anna’s Archive as a “notorious” online site (pdf). According to the publishers, traffic to Anna’s Archive’s domains grew 28% despite their enforcement efforts, to an average of 41 million visitors a month.

The AAP also highlights that Anna’s Archive offers AI developers high-speed access to its collection, in exchange for what the site describes as an “enterprise-level donation.”

Voice Clones and Leaks

The AI angle also applies to newcomer Lalals, a service operated by a company based in the United Arab Emirates. This AI platform allows users to change a vocal recording to sound like popular artists such as Taylor Swift and Drake, without their permission.

According to the RIAA, that infringes the artists’ rights of publicity and likely also infringes its members’ rights in the sound recordings that were used to train the voice models.

“The sound recording artists whose voices are being exploited include Taylor Swift, Drake, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Ed Sheeran, Lady Gaga, Chris Martin, and Rihanna, among many others,” RIAA writes.

Lalals

In the cyberlocker category, meanwhile, Mega is a familiar target. The European Commission added the file-hosting service to its own piracy watch list in 2022, and the RIAA now lists it among the notorious markets it wants the USTR to include.

“While Mega removes content that is specifically reported by rights holders, it does not implement effective measures to prevent the re-upload of infringing material or deter repeat infringement,” the RIAA writes.

RIAA stresses that users of the platform continue to share pre-release music and AI-related content, such as vocal models and cloned recordings. On what grounds Mega is required to prevent reuploads is not mentioned by the music group.

Several new cyberlockers are flagged for their role in pre-release piracy as well. These include Gofile, Sendgb and Imgur.gg.

Links to these services are reportedly shared on music leak forums, and the RIAA mentions Leaked.cx by name in the entries for Sendgb, Imgur.gg and Pixeldrain, which was already included in last year’s submission.

This Imgur.gg hosting platform doesn’t appear to be affiliated with the popular image host Imgur. When we checked, the site didn’t list any company details, but it did promote a music streaming app “Built by the imgur.gg team.”

Imgur.gg

RIAA goes on to mention that Telegram and Discord remain the primary mechanisms through which pre-release music is distributed. That accusation isn’t new, as the passage is nearly identical to last year’s submission.

Familiar Names, Familiar Words

Many other entries are familiar as well. The Pirate Bay, 1337x and RuTracker are listed in the torrent category, Rapidgator and Krakenfiles are flagged as cyberlockers, and Y2mate and Savefrom remain in the stream-ripping section.

Krakenfiles is still listed, even though the RIAA notes that it removed its upload functionality this year.

Whether any of the newly nominated sites will make it onto the USTR’s final list has yet to be seen. Last year, the USTR included several of the RIAA’s picks, including Y2mate, Savefrom and Krakenfiles.

Before the USTR makes its decision, the sites and services mentioned in the submissions can respond with rebuttals of their own, which Mega plans to do.

Responding to our request for comment, the company says that it removes reported content and permanently closes the accounts of repeat infringers, as is required under U.S. law.

According to Mega, infringing activity represents a small fraction of the overall use of the service. Last year, it processed close to 3.9 million copyright takedown requests and removed links represented around 0.002% of the more than 208 billion files stored by its 338 million registered users.

In the same period, 5,627 accounts were suspended under its “three strikes in six months” repeat infringer policy.

“Mega respectfully disagrees with the RIAA’s characterization, which fundamentally mischaracterizes the nature of the service, and will be filing its own submission with USTR setting out why its inclusion on the Notorious Markets List would be unwarranted,” Mega’s Legal and Compliance Manager Csaba Szabó informs TorrentFreak.

Last week, the RIAA responded with a submission that mostly mentions familiar targets. It lists torrent sites, stream-rippers and cyberlockers, many of which were flagged in previous years. There are some notable newcomers too, including Anna’s Archive.

Anna’s Archive and the Spotify Scrape

In December last year, the shadow library announced that it had downloaded 86 million music files from Spotify, plus metadata for 256 million tracks. This prompted an aggressive legal response.

A few days later, the RIAA coordinated an emergency court action on behalf of its members and Spotify, which resulted in a temporary restraining order against the site. Following this order, domain registry PIR suspended the site’s .org domain, and RIAA says Cloudflare also stopped providing services to the shadow library.

Following this crackdown, Anna’s Archive initially reported that its Spotify metadata torrent was “unavailable until further notice.” In February, however, the site quietly released roughly 3 million music files.

While the torrents for those releases were delisted shortly after, the lawsuit continued, with the labels and Spotify on the winning end.

“On April 14, 2026, RIAA and Spotify obtained a $322 million default judgment against the unknown operators of Anna’s Archive,” the RIAA writes in its USTR submission.

From RIAA’s submission

Despite the legal victory, the music group stresses that Anna’s Archive remains available through its .gl, .pk and .gd domains.

The RIAA isn’t the only rightsholder group that flagged the shadow library to the USTR. The Association of American Publishers (AAP) also lists Anna’s Archive as a “notorious” online site (pdf). According to the publishers, traffic to Anna’s Archive’s domains grew 28% despite their enforcement efforts, to an average of 41 million visitors a month.

The AAP also highlights that Anna’s Archive offers AI developers high-speed access to its collection, in exchange for what the site describes as an “enterprise-level donation.”

Voice Clones and Leaks

The AI angle also applies to newcomer Lalals, a service operated by a company based in the United Arab Emirates. This AI platform allows users to change a vocal recording to sound like popular artists such as Taylor Swift and Drake, without their permission.

According to the RIAA, that infringes the artists’ rights of publicity and likely also infringes its members’ rights in the sound recordings that were used to train the voice models.

“The sound recording artists whose voices are being exploited include Taylor Swift, Drake, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Ed Sheeran, Lady Gaga, Chris Martin, and Rihanna, among many others,” RIAA writes.

Lalals

In the cyberlocker category, meanwhile, Mega is a familiar target. The European Commission added the file-hosting service to its own piracy watch list in 2022, and the RIAA now lists it among the notorious markets it wants the USTR to include.

“While Mega removes content that is specifically reported by rights holders, it does not implement effective measures to prevent the re-upload of infringing material or deter repeat infringement,” the RIAA writes.

RIAA stresses that users of the platform continue to share pre-release music and AI-related content, such as vocal models and cloned recordings. On what grounds Mega is required to prevent reuploads is not mentioned by the music group.

Several new cyberlockers are flagged for their role in pre-release piracy as well. These include Gofile, Sendgb and Imgur.gg.

Links to these services are reportedly shared on music leak forums, and the RIAA mentions Leaked.cx by name in the entries for Sendgb, Imgur.gg and Pixeldrain, which was already included in last year’s submission.

This Imgur.gg hosting platform doesn’t appear to be affiliated with the popular image host Imgur. When we checked, the site didn’t list any company details, but it did promote a music streaming app “Built by the imgur.gg team.”

Imgur.gg

RIAA goes on to mention that Telegram and Discord remain the primary mechanisms through which pre-release music is distributed. That accusation isn’t new, as the passage is nearly identical to last year’s submission.

Familiar Names, Familiar Words

Many other entries are familiar as well. The Pirate Bay, 1337x and RuTracker are listed in the torrent category, Rapidgator and Krakenfiles are flagged as cyberlockers, and Y2mate and Savefrom remain in the stream-ripping section.

Krakenfiles is still listed, even though the RIAA notes that it removed its upload functionality this year.

Whether any of the newly nominated sites will make it onto the USTR’s final list has yet to be seen. Last year, the USTR included several of the RIAA’s picks, including Y2mate, Savefrom and Krakenfiles.

Before the USTR makes its decision, the sites and services mentioned in the submissions can respond with rebuttals of their own, which Mega plans to do.

Responding to our request for comment, the company says that it removes reported content and permanently closes the accounts of repeat infringers, as is required under U.S. law.

According to Mega, infringing activity represents a small fraction of the overall use of the service. Last year, it processed close to 3.9 million copyright takedown requests and removed links represented around 0.002% of the more than 208 billion files stored by its 338 million registered users.

In the same period, 5,627 accounts were suspended under its “three strikes in six months” repeat infringer policy.

item.title: VPNs and Cloudflare Escape beIN’s €10,000-a-Day Piracy Blocking Penalties
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

VPN providers and Cloudflare only have to make a reasonable effort to block pirate sports streams in France. That's the conclusion of two Paris court rulings that refused beIN Sports' request for penalties of €10,000 per day, per domain. Meanwhile, the Paris Court of Appeal put a separate VPN blocking appeal on hold until France's Supreme Court rules on DNS blocking.

In May, the Paris Judicial Court ordered several VPN providers to block ten pirate sites and IPTV services that streamed WTA tennis matches, including thetvapp.to and tennistream.com.

The order followed a familiar pattern. It was requested by beIN Sports, which holds the exclusive French rights to most WTA tour matches. A day later, the broadcaster secured a similar order against Cloudflare.

In its initial request, beIN asked for penalties of €2,000 per day for each domain that two of the VPN providers failed to block. The court refused to grant that, however, as nothing showed that the providers intended not to comply. If problems arose, the parties could return to court. That’s exactly what happened.

beIN Loses Penalty Request

As first reported by L’Informé, the broadcaster went back to the Paris court, complaining that VPN providers and Cloudflare had not fully blocked the sites. This time, it requested a daily penalty of €10,000 for every domain that remained accessible.

Cloudflare, Surfshark and NordVPN, all represented by the same lawyer, cited technical constraints and said they had done their best to comply. Proton was also targeted but did not show up at the hearing.

The blocking efforts were indeed not bulletproof. Cloudflare blocked three of the four sites, but only through its CDN. Surfshark and NordVPN blocked six of eleven, and only through the DNS service on their servers in France.

‘Reasonable Effort’

For the court, those measures were enough. In two rulings issued on October 7, it concluded that the intermediaries must make a reasonable effort to block the sites, but they don’t have to guarantee the outcome, in line with EU Court of Justice case law. The case files also showed that all companies had carried out the orders, at least in part.

“The requested penalty (…) therefore does not appear necessary or proportionate, given the need to strike a fair balance between the protection of the intellectual property rights of copyright and neighboring rights holders, and the freedom to conduct a business enjoyed by economic operators,” the court wrote, as quoted by L’Informé (translated).

The original blocking orders themselves remain in effect until the end of the WTA season, which is currently set for November 14. Meanwhile, beIN can still appeal.

The outcome mirrors the Paris court’s ruling in Canal+’s case against Cloudflare last month. There, Canal+ was refused daily penalties of €50,000 per site, as the court concluded that Cloudflare only had to take reasonable measures, which it did by blocking through its CDN.

DNS resolver Quad9 is next in line. According to the Swiss foundation, beIN wants €10,000 per domain, per day, which adds up to €580,000 a day. Quad9’s position is different, however, as it isn’t blocking any of the domains at all. A decision on that request is expected later this month.

Appeals Court Hits Pause

The penalty rulings are not the only setback for rightsholders. The VPN providers are also fighting the blocking orders directly, and that effort just got room to run.

Last year, NordVPN, Proton and CyberGhost appealed one of the first VPN blocking orders, which French football league LFP obtained in May 2025.

At the request of the VPN providers, the Paris Court of Appeal put that case on hold on September 30. Instead of ruling on the appeal, it will wait for France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation, to decide on appeals against seven earlier rulings.

These rulings, issued in March and May this year, upheld blocking orders that Canal+ obtained against DNS providers. In the March cases, Google, Cloudflare and Cisco lost their appeals. Several DNS providers then took the matter to the Supreme Court.

The appeals court acknowledged that these cases are not identical to the VPN dispute. However, it sees enough overlap to pause the case and wait for the Supreme Court outcome.

“Despite the differences, namely that the seven decisions under appeal concern DNS providers rather than VPNs, and that they were issued at the request of the Canal Plus companies rather than LFP and LFP1, the present case has many legal questions in common with the rulings under appeal before the [Supreme Court],” the court writes (translated).

From the freeze order

These overlapping questions include who can be ordered to help stop piracy, whether the French blocking law complies with EU law, how infringements must be proven, and when blocking measures are proportionate.

When the Supreme Court will rule on the matter is unknown, but the appeals court believes the outcome could affect the VPN case as well.

—

A copy of the Paris Court of Appeal’s ruling (RG 25/09229) is available here (pdf).

item.title: Chinese Court Jails Aiyifan Operator, U.S. Judge Won’t Transfer Pirate Site’s Domains
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits > Apps and Sites >

A Shanghai court confirmed the criminal conviction of Wang Jianyang, one of the operators of pirate streaming platform Aiyifan. In a parallel case, a Florida federal judge awarded Chinese streaming service iQIYI $1.96 million in damages, roughly 1% of what it initially requested. The court also refused to transfer Aiyifan’s domains, noting that the sites carry content from other rightsholders too.

Last month, Chinese streaming giant Tencent won the first round of its legal battle against the pirate site Olevod, when a Florida judge ruled that the case can proceed in the United States.

Tencent is not the only Chinese platform to try its luck there. Last year, rival streaming service iQIYI used the same court and the same legal team to sue Aiyifan, a pirate streaming service for Chinese speakers outside China.

Aiyifan also operates under the names YFSP and IYF, with domains including aiyifan.tv, yfsp.tv and iyf.tv. According to Similarweb, yfsp.tv alone drew roughly 14 million visits last month.

Unlike Olevod, Aiyifan never appeared in court, and none of its operators were named as defendants. However, the U.S. case isn’t the only legal trouble the pirate site is up against. In China, one of the site’s operators has been sentenced to prison recently.

Operator Jailed in China

In August, iQIYI informed the Florida court that the Shanghai Third Intermediate People’s Court had upheld the criminal conviction of Wang Jianyang, describing him as one of Aiyifan’s principals.

According to the ruling, Wang ran a company in Chongqing that provided the technical support for Aiyifan’s website and app. He also handled advertising and promotion, working on the pirate platform since 2022.

The Chinese police detained Wang in March 2024, which was more than a year before iQIYI filed its lawsuit in Florida.

Wang had been convicted before. In 2021, a court in Jiangsu gave him a suspended prison sentence of three years and a 6 million yuan fine for setting up another pirate site.

Aiyifan launched while he was still on probation. In March of this year, a Shanghai district court revoked the suspension and added a new sentence of three and a half years, plus a 1 million yuan fine. Combined, Wang faces four and a half years in prison and a 7 million yuan fine.

From the translated Shanghai ruling

Wang appealed the verdict, arguing that the evidence was insufficient and that, at most, he merely provided technical support. The appeals court disagreed, however, concluding that he played a major role in the operation. That ruling is final.

Florida: $1.96 Million Instead of $196 Million

In Florida, iQIYI’s civil case was launched in hopes to shut down the site. Aiyifan didn’t respond to the complaint in the U.S. federal court, after which a default was entered in July 2025.

iQIYI asked for a massive $196.55 million in damages. Most of that came from applying the $150,000 statutory maximum to 776 registered works, while thousands of unregistered works added another $78.55 million in proposed damages.

In January, Judge Melissa Damian ruled that Aiyifan is indeed liable. However, she rejected the damages award because it lacked support. iQIYI responded with a revised request for $54.4 million, but that was still too much for the court.

In an order issued last week, Judge Damian awarded $1,000 per registered work, doubled for willfulness, for a total of $1.8 million. The award covers a total of 901 works as more copyright registrations had been processed as the case moved on.

The trademark claims added $160,000, but there were no damages awarded for the roughly 5,000 unregistered works. This brings the total to $1.96 million, about 1% of the original request.

From the final default judgment

The reduces damages is not the only setback for the Chinese streaming company either, as its requested injunction is also limited.

Judge Won’t Transfer Domains

iQIYI specifically targeted the pirate site’s domain names, asking the court to hand them over and redirect them to iQIYI’s own site. It also wanted ISPs, hosting companies, CDNs, payment processors and WeChat to stop serving Aiyifan.

The amended motion for a default judgment dropped most of these third parties, but it still requested the domain takeovers, to effectively take these offline.

Judge Damian was not convinced that this would be appropriate. iQIYI admitted that it couldn’t say how much of the content on the sites was infringing, or whether any of the other content is licensed.

Aiyifan streams plenty of content that is not owned by iQIYI. Taking over the domains entirely would therefore go too far, the judge concluded.

The order acknowledges that “some other judges in this District have a more liberal approach to the dispensation of injunctive relief.” However, Judge Damian sided with the Eleventh Circuit’s requirement that injunctions must be narrowly tailored.

yfsp.tv’s homepage this week, with Toy Story 5 in the top slot

Partial Domain Registrar Suspensions?

Instead of transferring the domains, the judgment orders domain registrars to cancel the pages and subdomains that feature iQIYI’s shows or trademarks, once iQIYI provides a list.

If a registrar fails to comply, the registry must move the domain to a registrar of iQIYI’s choosing. That changes the registrar but would not transfer the ownership.

The registrar provisions in the judgment

Whether registrars can comply is questionable. A registrar controls the domain registration, not the pages on a website, so the only tools at its disposal are suspending or redirecting a domain as a whole.

That is exactly the broad outcome the court is trying to avoid.

Even the subdomains are a stretch. Two of the listed sites, m.yfsp.tv and www.yfsp.tv, share a single domain, and a registrar can only switch one of them off if it also runs the domain’s DNS.

For now, the Aiyifan sites remain online. Without a response from the operators, it’s also unclear whether iQIYI will be able to collect any of the damages.

—

A copy of the final default judgment, issued at the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, is available here (pdf). The accompanying order can be found here (pdf), and the translated Shanghai ruling, as filed by iQIYI, here (pdf).

The seven (sub)domains listed in the judgment: m.yfsp.tv, www.yfsp.tv, www.yfsp.lv, www.iyf.tv, www.iyf.lv, www.aiyifan.tv and www.ayysp.com.

item.title: Court Approves ‘voices38’ Subpoenas After Denuvo Drops Payment and Login Data Requests
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

Denuvo can subpoena Discord, Valve and Reddit to identify the anonymous game cracker ‘voices38’. After a California federal judge raised privacy concerns, the DRM company dropped its demands for payment data, comments and other data, reducing 46 requests to nine. What remains are identity and contact details, including IP addresses, which Denuvo says may be the only reliable path to identify the defendant.

Earlier this month, Denuvo asked a California federal court for help to unmask the person or group behind the popular game cracking handle ‘voices38’.

The request is part of the DMCA anti-circumvention lawsuit that the Irdeto-owned company filed in September. That complaint identified the cracker only by a Discord user ID, a Reddit account and seven Steam profiles.

Denuvo wanted to subpoena Discord, Valve and Reddit, and its request wasn’t limited to just names and email addresses. The proposed subpoenas also requested payment details, login logs and post/comment histories, which turned out to be a step too far for the court.

‘Voluminous Data’

On October 8, Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. ordered Denuvo to explain why it needs “the voluminous data contained in its requests for production” to identify and serve the defendant.

“Plaintiff’s requests for production go well beyond what is needed for the limited purpose of identifying the defendant and could pose substantial privacy concerns,” Judge Gilliam wrote.

Privacy concerns

The proposed subpoena to Valve was the broadest with 35 requests for the seven Steam profiles. These covered payment methods and transaction histories, IP addresses with timestamps, device identifiers, and any linked accounts.

Discord was asked to list the account’s server memberships and role assignments. Reddit, meanwhile, was asked for the posts and comments by ‘voices38’, as well as the account’s subreddit memberships.

From 46 Requests to Nine

The judge gave Denuvo the option to revise the subpoenas, using a narrow subpoena model from another case, or justify each data request in detail.

Denuvo chose the revise option. A few days ago, it filed new subpoenas that ask the platforms for targeted information.

Each request now covers documents relating to the identity or contact information of the account holder. That includes names, identification documents, email addresses, IP addresses, phone numbers, and business or residential addresses. Instead of the 46 original requests, there are now nine.

Info requested from Reddit

The new requests no longer list payment data, transaction histories, login logs, comments or posts. They do ask for IP addresses and phone numbers, which go beyond the model subpoena the judge pointed to. Denuvo argues that the platforms collect little information at sign up, and that what they collect is self reported.

The IP addresses may therefore be the only reliable path to the defendant, Denuvo writes. It also wants any name or identification document these companies have on file.

“Denuvo has only a pseudonym,” the company notes.

The nine requests

# Platform Target Account / Identifier Information Demanded

Privacy concerns

item.title: Judge Orders Meta to Name Employees Who Approved Torrenting Anna’s Archive and LibGen
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

Meta will have to name the people who greenlit its torrenting of pirated books. A federal magistrate judge has ordered the company to identify everyone who approved sourcing books from LibGen and Anna’s Archive. This goes beyond the employees who ran the downloads and includes whoever decided whether to seed the books to others.

Last month, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixson ordered Meta to hand over the command histories of the servers it used to torrent pirated books.

These logs would presumably reveal how Meta’s torrent clients were set up, including any changes to their upload settings.

The order is one of many discovery battles in the lawsuits over Meta’s use of shadow libraries. In the class action filed by authors including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman, the court already ruled that training AI models on the books was fair use. That left the BitTorrent claims as the last live part of that case.

The server logs could reveal what happened on Meta’s machines. However, publisher Entrepreneur Media also wants to know who approved the torrenting activity.

‘Technical’ Decisions

Entrepreneur Media, which publishes Entrepreneur magazine, filed one of the related lawsuits where it accuses Meta of contributing to piracy by uploading (seeding) works to third parties, similar to the authors’ contributory infringement claim.

To find out more, the publisher asked Meta to identify everyone who “made, authorized, or approved” the decisions to obtain the shadow library datasets, and to do so via BitTorrent.

Meta’s answers named several people who are believed to have been involved in data-related decisions. However, Meta said it couldn’t identify anyone who “formally” made or approved decisions to acquire or use books for its first two Llama models. Those decisions were often the result of team consensus, Meta argued.

When it came to the torrenting itself, Meta pointed to the employees who ran the downloads, describing their choices as technical decisions.

Decision?

Meta added that the acquisition of data from Anna’s Archive went through an internal legal review in early 2024, which involved its in-house lawyers.

In other words, the company didn’t name anyone higher up who approved the use of BitTorrent.

“On that construction no one at Meta decided to torrent anything, yet Meta torrented shadow libraries repeatedly from 2022-2024,” Entrepreneur Media countered.

‘Legally Not Okay’

The question becomes more concrete when it comes to seeding. One of the engineers who torrented LibGen data previously testified that the issue of seeding was raised and discussed internally, and that steps were taken to limit it.

An internal Meta logbook, which one employee reviewed before starting a download from Anna’s Archive, mentions a decision not to use torrents.

“Decided to go with direct file uploads without using torrents for the following reasons: Using torrents would entail seeding the file such as sharing content outside. This would be legally not okay,” the logbook reads, as quoted in Entrepreneur Media’s filing.

‘Legally not okay’

Meta does not deny that it used BitTorrent to download LibGen’s Scimag collection and data from Anna’s Archive. However, it says it isn’t aware of anyone who “made, authorized, or approved” a decision to upload or distribute the data. Meta’s lawyers also added that measures were implemented to avoid seeding.

How much data Meta shared with others is not clear either. Last year, Meta’s own expert estimated that uploads from its AWS servers didn’t exceed roughly 30% of the data downloaded during torrent downloads between April and July 2024.

Everyone in the Group

Yesterday, Judge Hixson ruled on the dispute. Two weeks earlier, Meta informed the court that it had no additional information to provide on the torrenting decision.

This didn’t convince the judge. He noted that the interrogatory isn’t limited to formal decisions, and that Meta’s answers were mostly about using the data, not obtaining or downloading it.

Meta’s argument that decisions were often collaborative doesn’t change that. The interrogatory asks about all decisionmakers, so if a decision was made by a team, everyone involved has to be named.

Everyone in the group

Meta must also identify the people who took part in the discussion that preceded the 2023 LibGen torrent download. In addition, it has to name the people who approved going ahead with BitTorrent, and whoever greenlit the April 2024 download from Anna’s Archive.

Notably, the order also covers everyone who decided “whether or how to seed, or to mitigate seeding,” when Meta downloaded LibGen’s Scimag collection and Anna’s Archive through BitTorrent.

For Entrepreneur Media, these names are important. The publisher says the answers “bear on” willfulness, as well as on its contributory copyright infringement and distribution claims.

This dispute largely revolved around naming the people involved. Whether Meta’s torrenting was fair use, and whether it actually distributed pirated books to others, has yet to be decided.

—

A copy of Magistrate Judge Hixson’s order is available here (pdf). The joint letter briefs filed by Entrepreneur Media and Meta can be found here (pdf) and here (pdf). Meta’s second supplemental interrogatory responses are available here (pdf).

item.title: ‘VPNs at Risk’: Tech Coalition Pushes Back on Piracy Blocking Duties for VPNs
item.description:
Home > Technology > VPN Providers >

A new report published by the Internet Infrastructure Coalition (i2Coalition) warns that poorly targeted VPN regulation can weaken the security infrastructure everyone depends on. The group, whose members include VPN providers, points to piracy blocking orders against VPNs in France, while U.S. lawmakers also consider similar blocking requirements. The report is released on Global Encryption Day.

When Rep. Darrell Issa introduced his site blocking bill last month, VPN providers made the list.

The American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA) would allow courts to order ISPs, DNS resolvers, and VPNs to block foreign pirate sites.

The competing DEFEND IP Act, introduced days later by Rep. Zoe Lofgren and Sen. Thom Tillis, does the opposite. It explicitly excludes services that only offer VPNs.

The VPN industry has a voice in U.S. blocking debates through the Internet Infrastructure Coalition (i2Coalition). In addition to representing companies such as Amazon, Cloudflare, and Google, the group runs a VPN Trust Initiative, with ExpressVPN, NordVPN, and Surfshark as founding members.

The coalition has been relatively quiet in recent site blocking discussions, but today, on Global Encryption Day, i2Coalition published a report titled “VPNs at Risk.”

Like last year’s DNS at Risk report, it warns against turning neutral infrastructure into a copyright enforcement tool.

VPNs at Risk

From Pirate Sites to VPNs

Copyright enforcement is one of the reasons governments consider regulating VPNs, the report notes. VPNs can be used to bypass blocking measures and may make it harder for rightsholders to identify infringers or enforce geographic licensing restrictions.

France has been one of the prime examples of this type of regulation, i2Coalition notes. In May 2025, a Paris court ordered NordVPN, CyberGhost, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Proton VPN to block 203 pirate sports streaming domains at the request of Canal+.

More orders followed later.

“These cases, brought by rightsholders before French courts, illustrate how obligations imposed at one layer of the Internet can migrate to another when users find alternative technical paths around court-ordered restrictions,” the report notes.

Migrating obligations

That raises a broader question.

According to the report, the issue is not just which intermediaries can be ordered to block, but whether these measures actually reduce piracy, and what side effects they have for lawful users.

The French legal battle isn’t over either.

The report describes the decisions as “currently pending appeal,” but it doesn’t mention the latest twists. On September 30, the Paris Court of Appeal put an appeal by NordVPN, Proton, and CyberGhost against a similar order, obtained by football league LFP, on hold. It will first wait for a ruling from France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation, in related DNS blocking cases.

A week later, the Paris court refused beIN’s request for daily penalties against VPN providers and Cloudflare, which had not fully blocked the targeted sites.

i2Coalition is aware of these developments but will keep the report text as is.

“We’re following those proceedings, including the pending Cour de cassation outcome. We’re keeping the text for this release, but those developments will inform future updates. They don’t change our broader concern about the implications of extending blocking obligations to VPN providers,” Executive Director Christian Dawson tells us.

Target the Right Layer

The report doesn’t ask for a VPN exemption from any and all regulation. Instead, it urges lawmakers to be precise, and to take measures where they make the most sense.

“Policymakers should consider where meaningful knowledge and control actually reside and whether an obligation can be directed toward the relevant conduct or service before moving deeper into general-purpose Internet infrastructure. The further an intervention moves from the activity being regulated, the greater the need to consider its effects on unrelated users and services,” the report reads.

Target the right layer

Targeting the right layer is particularly important when it comes to VPNs. Consumer VPN services and corporate networks rely on many of the same underlying technologies, including protocols such as OpenVPN and WireGuard.

The report notes that Russia’s reported blocking of these VPN protocols shows how hard it is to tell the different uses apart at the network level.

When it comes to liability, i2Coalition points to the U.S. Supreme Court’s Cox ruling from earlier this year. This ruling confirmed that continuing to provide an Internet service, while knowing that some customers may misuse it, isn’t enough on its own to establish contributory copyright infringement.

The group sees the principles from this ruling as relevant to VPNs as well, but it doesn’t claim the matter is settled.

“If providers face liability merely because general-purpose services can be misused, they may have strong incentives to terminate users, restrict access, or intervene preemptively even when they have limited knowledge of the underlying conduct. Obligations should therefore reflect what an intermediary can reasonably know, control, and address,” the report warns.

Strong incentives

“We see those principles as relevant to the debate around VPNs, but we aren’t suggesting that the ruling automatically determines the outcome of every VPN case. That would depend on the facts and legal issues presented,” Dawson notes.

VPN providers are not completely without responsibilities. According to the report, they can strengthen trust through independent audits and cooperation with legitimate legal processes. Voluntary programs, such as the VPN Trust Initiative’s own Trust Seal, can complement these efforts.

Lawmakers, in turn, should involve VPN providers and other technical experts from the start when they want to tackle a problem.

Silent on U.S. Bills

The report doesn’t apply these recommendations to the pending site blocking bills, as neither ACPA nor DEFEND IP is mentioned.

That’s notable, as ACPA would allow courts to name VPN providers with 100,000 or more monthly U.S. users or subscribers in a blocking order. That’s a position VPN companies would rather not be in.

TorrentFreak asked i2Coalition why the report doesn’t mention the two bills. Dawson says that the group is following both proposals, but that this particular report focuses on other developments.

“For this edition, we’ve focused on the developments covered in the report rather than trying to capture every pending legislative proposal. We expect to revisit US legislation in a future update as the debate develops,” Dawson says.

For now, both bills remain pending. Issa retires at the end of the year and Tillis’s term ends in January, so both bills would have to move ahead before the current session closes.

—

A copy of i2Coalition’s “VPNs at Risk” report is available here (pdf).

item.title: DNS Resolver Quad9 Will Leave France After Court Orders Piracy Blocking Penalty
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

Quad9 is leaving France over pirate site blocking orders, which makes it the second DNS resolver to leave the country. Quad9 will stop serving French users on November 24, after a Paris court set a €1,000 daily penalty for not blocking pirate tennis streams. Faced with this order and roughly 20 other pending French cases, Quad9 says that it has no other viable option left.

Earlier this month, DNS resolver Quad9 informed TorrentFreak that it was weighing its future in France, including the option to leave the country altogether.

The Swiss non-profit foundation faced a request from beIN Sports for penalties of up to €580,000 a day, as Quad9 chose not to block pirate tennis streams.

Yesterday the Paris Court ruled on the matter and not in favor of Quad9. As a direct result, the foundation decided that it will no longer offer its services to users in France starting November 24.

Farewell, France

€1,000 a Day

The court ordered Quad9 to implement the May blocking order, which since expanded to 58 domain names, or face a penalty of €1,000 a day, which is a fraction of beIN’s demands.

beIN had asked for €10,000 per day for every domain that remained accessible through Quad9. The court set the penalty at €1,000 per day in total instead. This runs until the blocking measures end on November 14, which Quad9 calculates adds up to €24,000, not counting its own legal costs.

Quad9 told us that it understands it is now subject to the penalty, as it won’t block the domains before the order ends.

In its ruling, the court points to Quad9’s own statements. According to the court, Quad9 has to make reasonable efforts to block the domain names, but it decided to take no action at all, for reasons it previously explained.

Reasonable effort

That’s a different outcome than earlier this month, when the Paris court refused beIN’s penalty requests against Cloudflare and several VPN providers. These companies had blocked at least some of the domains, which the court considered a reasonable effort.

Canal+ also lost a similar penalty request against Cloudflare in September. Quad9, however, hasn’t blocked a single domain, as it also confirmed in a statement submitted to the court.

Leaving France

For Quad9, the case was never just about money. The foundation sees recursive DNS resolution as a neutral service and doesn’t want to tamper with it.

“We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations,” Quad9 writes in a statement.

The Swiss foundation also says that it can’t accurately block for French users only. Its free service requires no sign-up and it says that there is no reliable way to tell which users are in France.

Blocking the domains for all users would also satisfy the court, Quad9 confirms. However, the DNS resolver refuses to apply a French court order to Internet users worldwide.

How Quad9 will stop serving French users hasn’t been decided yet. The foundation told us that it’s still evaluating its options, which it believes are all imperfect.

Blocking wouldn’t help much either, Quad9 argues, as there are plenty of workarounds. People who want to access the pirate sites can simply switch to one of the thousands of other open DNS resolvers.

“This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert,” the foundation says.

More Blocking Cases

The decision to leave isn’t just about this beIN case. Quad9 notes that roughly 20 other blocking cases are pending in France and the foundation expects many of them to ultimately lead to more blocking pressure and potential fines.

“Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN,” it notes.

Cannot survive

Quad9 isn’t the first public DNS resolver to make this move. In 2024, OpenDNS suspended its service in France in response to a Canal+ blocking order.

Quad9 will stop serving French users on November 24, after a Paris court set a €1,000 daily penalty for not blocking pirate tennis streams. Faced with this order and roughly 20 other pending French cases, Quad9 says that it has no other viable option left.

Earlier this month, DNS resolver Quad9 informed TorrentFreak that it was weighing its future in France, including the option to leave the country altogether.

The Swiss non-profit foundation faced a request from beIN Sports for penalties of up to €580,000 a day, as Quad9 chose not to block pirate tennis streams.

Yesterday the Paris Court ruled on the matter and not in favor of Quad9. As a direct result, the foundation decided that it will no longer offer its services to users in France starting November 24.

Farewell, France

€1,000 a Day

The court ordered Quad9 to implement the May blocking order, which since expanded to 58 domain names, or face a penalty of €1,000 a day, which is a fraction of beIN’s demands.

Quad9 told us that it understands it is now subject to the penalty, as it won’t block the domains before the order ends.

In its ruling, the court points to Quad9’s own statements. According to the court, Quad9 has to make reasonable efforts to block the domain names, but it decided to take no action at all, for reasons it previously explained.

That’s a different outcome than earlier this month, when the Paris court refused beIN’s penalty requests against Cloudflare and several VPN providers. These companies had blocked at least some of the domains, which the court considered a reasonable effort.
