item.title: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist
item.description:
Home > Opinion Articles >

A fresh academic paper on Z-Library cites a TorrentFreak article that doesn’t exist, and several other sources in the paper are also unfindable. The authors disclose that they used AI tools, which may explain what is going on. The use of AI in an academic paper on shadow libraries is also somewhat ironic, as rightsholders are suing AI companies for using these sites to train AI models.

Z-Library is one of the largest pirate ebook libraries on the Internet, offering millions of books and papers for free.

For students and researchers who can’t afford expensive textbooks and journal subscriptions, it can be a useful resource. At the same time, publishers have spent years trying to take it down, with takedown notices and blocking orders, while U.S. authorities indicted its alleged operators.

This tension is the subject of a paper published earlier this month in the journal New Review of Academic Librarianship, written by two librarians at Nigerian universities.

The paper

The peer-reviewed academic paper doesn’t pick a side and the lead author kindly shared a copy of their work with TorrentFreak. While the conclusions are not immediately newsworthy, there was one reference that stood out right away.

A TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist

In a section on enforcement against Z-Library, the authors write that major academic publishers, including Elsevier and Springer Nature, have taken similar legal action. The reference is a 2021 TorrentFreak article, as shown below.

The claim

The problem is that this particular legal action is new to us. The reference section lists the article as “Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries” and links to the TorrentFreak homepage. However, we have never published an article with that title.

We did report that Elsevier and Springer Nature obtained a UK blocking order against Sci-Hub, and that several Z-Library domains were temporarily suspended over copyright infringement claims. However, we’re not aware of this particular legal action against Z-Library.

Looking more closely, we see more claims that don’t seem to fit. The paper’s account of the Z-Library criminal case, for example, states that the U.S. Department of Justice “arrested individuals” in 2022.

Some references

The DOJ’s own press release says that the two alleged operators, whose indictment we covered at the time, were arrested in Argentina “at the request of the United States.” The title the paper gives for that press release doesn’t exist either.

Plausible but Inaccurate

These non-existent citations appear plausible, as they cite real publications and organizations in a fitting context. However, that doesn’t mean they are accurate. When we went over the full reference list, we noticed that this applies to more sources.

The paper cites a 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology article by IP law professor Daniel Gervais, titled “The future of intellectual property in the shadow of shadow libraries.” The table of contents of the cited issue doesn’t include it, and the cited pages are taken up by two articles on other topics.

The same applies to a 2019 College & Research Libraries article attributed to Carol Tenopir and colleagues. The cited issue has no article by Tenopir. She did co-author a 2019 article on a similar topic, but it appeared in a different journal, under a different title.

Other references that couldn’t be located include a 2019 article credited to Björn Brembs and articles credited to authors named Smith, Piper, Okike and Aronson, as well as a Kaspersky report on “the hidden dangers of shadow libraries.”

In total, we had trouble finding at least ten of the 44 references in the paper, as well as others that didn’t necessarily back the stated claims.

100% AI?

The obvious question is where these mystery references came from. The paper’s acknowledgements may offer a hint in the right direction, as they mention that AI was used in the research and writing process.

“We confirm that Consensus AI was used in sifting through large volume of literature and extract relevant information,” the authors write. They add that ChatGPT was used to improve the language of parts of the paper.

Acknowledgements

AI chatbots are known to invent references, often with plausible titles credited to real experts in the field. This could explain the findings, although it doesn’t prove that AI wrote these references.

We also ran the paper’s abstract and conclusion through the AI detection tool Pangram. For both sections, the tool reported that “100% of the text is likely AI-generated.” These types of tools are not perfect and can produce false positives, but it would fit the picture.

Pangram’s conclusion

It would be rather ironic if AI caused these errors. It would mean that a paper in a commercial, peer-reviewed journal, published by Taylor & Francis, relied on AI to write about Z-Library. Meanwhile, many rightsholders are suing AI companies for using shadow libraries to train AI models.

Interestingly, the paper explicitly warns that sites such as Z-Library hurt publishers’ revenue, which funds peer review and editing.

“The widespread use of Z-Library poses significant challenges to the sustainability of academic publishing. Publishers rely on subscription fees and paywalls to fund the peer review, editing, and distribution of scholarly works,” it reads, presumably generated by AI as well.

The paper doesn’t mention that peer reviewers generally aren’t paid for their work, an issue that was central to a recent lawsuit against major academic publishers, including Taylor & Francis.

Publisher Investigates

The lead author initially shared a copy of the paper with us, but didn’t answer our follow-up questions about the mysterious references. We also asked Gervais, Brembs and Tenopir whether they wrote the papers that are credited to them, but they didn’t respond either.

Publisher Taylor & Francis did reply and says that it’s looking into the matter.

“I can confirm that this has been referred to our Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams, who will investigate the concerns you have raised,” a Taylor & Francis spokesperson informed TorrentFreak.

The publisher will not comment further while the investigation is ongoing. Whether the paper will be corrected or retracted has yet to be seen.

—

The paper “Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?” is available here.

item.title: Framing the News: Anti-Piracy Press Release Turned a 2016 Raid Into a 2026 Story (2016)
item.description:
Home > Opinion Articles >

In August, City of London Police and anti-piracy group FACT announced a six and a half year prison sentence for a 68-year-old pirate IPTV operator. Without dates or a service name in the release, some outlets reported it as a recent bust. Records obtained by TorrentFreak show the operation was raided in 2016, the operator pleaded guilty, and the service was called Ex Pat TV.

On August 27, City of London Police published a press release headlined: “Man in his 60s jailed for 6.5 years after making over £980,000 through illegal streaming.”

In the days that followed, this exact framing was repeated throughout many online news articles.

The release came with statements from the Federation Against Copyright Theft (FACT), the Premier League, Sky and BBC Studios. Additionally, FACT published the same release on its own website the next day.

Headlines

City of London Police said that a 68-year-old from Chorley was “found guilty of conspiracy to defraud” at Preston Crown Court. His business ran on 80 servers, sold subscriptions to customers worldwide, particularly British expats, and generated £980,812 “over a three-year period.”

As is often the case with UK enforcement efforts, details are scarce. The official press releases didn’t mention the pirate service at stake, nor did they say anything about when these offenses took place, or what the reasoning of the court was.

Some news reports filled in these blanks themselves. The Mirror, for example, used the following headline: “Massive streaming crackdown blocks more UK homes from watching Sky for free.”

The Mirror reported that a “major closure has taken place after a man behind a popular illegal streaming service was recently arrested.” The server seizure left customers “with nothing more than blank screens,” it added, suggesting that this was a recent action.

The Mirror, September 1

IBC reported that all 80 servers “have now been seized,” and a French site wrote that British justice had “just dismantled” the operation. Meanwhile, BleepingComputer suggested the seized servers “may lead to the identification of users” who could face fines.

After some digging, we can now confirm that this case isn’t recent at all. In fact, the raid on Ibrahim’s operation dates back to 2016, more than a decade ago.

Pleaded Guilty

The release got the three-year period right, but the rest of the picture looks different.

After several emails and a check of our press credentials, Preston Crown Court confirmed that Ibrahim pleaded guilty to two counts. For the indictment, the court referred us to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which also named the service and answered follow-up questions, partly on background.

According to the CPS, Ibrahim pleaded guilty five days into his trial.

A guilty plea sounds different than being “found guilty”. When we asked the City of London Police about the wording in its press release, it said: “The jury did find him guilty but he plead guilty before. The terminology is fine to use for either.”

When a defendant changes his plea after the jury has been sworn in, the jury is typically asked to return a formal guilty verdict. The conviction rests on the plea.

Which Three Years?

The indictment also fills in the dates, revealing that this case is far from new. All three counts run from June 1, 2013 to August 10, 2016.

That end date is the day of a raid. On August 10, 2016, PIPCU searched a business and three homes in Chorley and arrested three men, aged 36, 40 and 58, on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud and money laundering. Ibrahim was 58 at the time. The 2026 release does not mention this raid.

From the indictment

TorrentFreak reported on the raid the next day. At the time, sources already pointed to a Chorley company selling IPTV packages to expats.

The CPS now confirms that the previously unnamed service was “initially known as ‘Ex Pat TV’ and latterly ‘My TV Abroad’.” This rebrand happened before the raid.

With those names, TorrentFreak was able to locate the service’s old website. An archived copy of mytvabroad.com from July 15, 2016, less than four weeks before the raid, carries a banner announcing the switch: “BIG RE-BRAND! Ex-Pat TV is now My TV Abroad.”

My TV Abroad, July 2016

The site promised “live UK channels, anywhere in the world” from £19 per month, with no VPN required. Its footer credits a web designer in Chorley.

That means FACT’s identification of the service, which it highlighted in the release, took place more than a decade ago. That wasn’t mentioned either. There’s more new information too.

From Three Defendants to One

The press release mentions just one defendant, but the indictment names three. In addition to Milan Ibrahim, it lists two other men, who were also charged with conspiracy to defraud copyright holders, through live TV streams, movie streams and satellite decoders supplied to commercial premises.

Milan Ibrahim pleaded guilty to the first two counts but the other two men were not convicted. The Crown did not proceed against either of them. TorrentFreak understands that Milan Ibrahim was seen as the main instigator, and that the case against the other two was resolved as part of his plea. The exact arrangement hasn’t been confirmed.

None of the new information changes the outcome. Ibrahim is serving six and a half years and, according to the police, faces Proceeds of Crime Act proceedings to recover the £980,812. That was all clear from the press release.

For proper news reporting, however, context is key. That the pirate IPTV service, Ex Pat TV or My TV Abroad, was raided a decade ago, and that the sentence followed a guilty plea, are not trivial details. The same is true for the co-defendants, who were part of the same indictment.

Why the police and FACT left these details out is unknown.

—

A copy of the revised indictment in R v Ibrahim and others (Preston Crown Court, T20237377) is available here (pdf). The names of the two co-defendants, who were not convicted, have been redacted.

item.title: Meta Pitches AI Sports Piracy Detector in Notorious Markets Rebuttal
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

Meta informed the U.S. Trade Representative that it built an AI tool to predict whether a live stream is a pirated sports broadcast. The tool is featured in Meta’s rebuttal to this year’s “notorious markets” submissions, which also lists restrictions on Facebook Live. Cloud storage platform Mega, meanwhile, rejects piracy accusations in its rebuttal but acknowledges that its repeat infringer system didn't work properly for months.

Earlier this month, rightsholders sent their annual overviews of “notorious” piracy markets to the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR).

The MPA, RIAA and other groups listed dozens of pirate sites, but online platforms and infrastructure providers were mentioned too. Several of them have now responded with rebuttals of their own.

This includes Meta, whose rebuttal mostly addresses counterfeiting concerns. However, unlike last year, the company also dedicates a section to piracy, much of it focused on unauthorized live streams.

AI-Predicted Pirate Streams

Meta describes a three-pronged response to piracy. It aims to stop infringing content from being posted, remove what gets through, and make the rest harder to find. According to the company, its recent efforts against live streaming piracy show that this approach works.

The most prominent example is a new AI tool that spots pirated sports broadcasts while they are being streamed.

“[I]n 2026, we built and launched an advanced AI enforcement tool that analyzes video content along with additional signals, to predict whether the content is an unauthorized stream of a professional sports broadcast,” Meta writes.

“Based on the prediction results, we can proactively remove this content in real time, before it gains a significant audience, and without a rights holder ever having to intervene.”

AI enforcement

Meta doesn’t share any figures on the AI tool, such as how many streams it removed or which sports events it was used for.

IPTV and Firestick Warnings

The AI tool works alongside changes to Facebook Live. New accounts are not allowed to use Live at all, and most users can only host a limited number of streams at the same time. Accounts that had a live stream blocked are limited in the features they can use.

Pop-ups

item.title: Judge Allows Google, Yahoo and Microsoft Subpoenas to Identify Gay-Torrents Users
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

FlavaWorks can subpoena Google, Yahoo, Microsoft and three other companies to identify staff and members of the defunct BitTorrent site Gay-Torrents.org, an Illinois federal court ruled. Instead of starting from IP addresses, the subpoenas target the email accounts that are linked to their tracker profiles. How FlavaWorks obtained those email addresses remains unclear.

Earlier this year, adult entertainment company FlavaWorks sued the operators and hundreds of users of private torrent tracker Gay-Torrents.org.

The lawsuit had an immediate effect, as the tracker went offline shortly after. In an amended complaint, FlavaWorks later narrowed its list of targeted users from 325 to 39.

Several of the site’s administrators and most of the targeted members are still listed as anonymous John Does. To change that, FlavaWorks asked the court for permission to subpoena their email providers. In an October 14 order, U.S. District Judge John Robert Blakey granted this request in part.

Subpoenas Target Google, Yahoo, Microsoft

The order allows FlavaWorks to subpoena Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, AT&T, Cloudflare and Newfold Digital. Each subpoena is limited to the email addresses or domains of defendants linked to that provider.

The targeted services are asked to hand over the subscriber’s name, mailing address and phone number, as well as any secondary, recovery or two-factor authentication email addresses. FlavaWorks can also request the most recent IP address that was used to access each account, covering the period from January 2025 onward.

The order

The judge didn’t give FlavaWorks carte blanche. The company also asked for the billing names and addresses on file with the email providers, and for a subpoena to payment processor Stripe to identify the people behind a Bulgarian company linked to the site. The order includes neither.

An IP Address Is Not a Person

Subpoenas targeting email providers are not common in torrent-related lawsuits. Rightsholders typically collect IP addresses from torrent swarms and ask Internet providers to identify the account holders. FlavaWorks says it has IP address data for the defendants too, but it chose to go after their email accounts instead, bypassing the more common ISP route.

As justification, FlavaWorks mentions an argument that’s usually reserved for defendants, stating that an IP address is not a person.

“But an IP address identifies an Internet subscription, not a person: it resolves to whoever pays the bill for a household, an office, a university network, or a shared carrier-grade address pool, and it can be masked by a VPN,” FlavaWorks writes.

Not a person

An email address, the company argues, is personal to the account holder, which should help to identify the defendants.

According to the exhibit filed with the motion, 22 defendants are linked to Gmail addresses, nine to Yahoo, three to Hotmail and one to an AT&T address. Two others use private domains, registered through Cloudflare and Bluehost, a Newfold Digital company.

Email providers

This list of targets isn’t limited to regular members. Several of the site’s administrators are on it as well, identified by Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail addresses. One other administrator, who used a ProtonMail address, was left out, as the Swiss company is beyond the reach of a U.S. subpoena.

Tracker Users Can Still Object

The new order doesn’t mean that the data will be handed over right away. It explicitly allows the defendants and the providers to move to quash the subpoenas.

Google, for example, has pushed back before. In February, we reported that the company raised First Amendment concerns over a similar FlavaWorks subpoena targeting users of another private tracker.

However, in a July filing, FlavaWorks said that Google produced subscriber data in that case in April. Whether that covered all the targeted Gmail accounts is not mentioned. FlavaWorks adds that the tech giant handed over the same type of information in an earlier case, without objection.

Insider Knowledge?

For FlavaWorks, the subpoenas are meant to confirm its existing suspicions. The member defendants in this case were selected because the email address on their tracker account matched an account on one of FlavaWorks’ own sites.

In a September status report, the company said that its own records already point to a probable identity for many of them. It doesn’t want to name anyone publicly, however, before the email providers confirm who is behind each account.

How FlavaWorks obtained the email addresses in the first place is still a mystery. On an invite-only tracker, this information is typically only visible to staff. The court filings don’t offer a direct answer but cite the company’s own records and “investigation” without going into detail.

The September status report, which we haven’t seen reported anywhere, shows that FlavaWorks has help, presumably from an insider.

“Plaintiff has also obtained the cooperation of an individual with direct knowledge of the Site’s operation,” it reads.

Direct knowledge

The report doesn’t say when this cooperation started, or whether this person is the source of the email addresses. That said, FlavaWorks expects that this cooperation can help identify the operators, as well as other users who shared its works or funded the site.

Some defendants are already settling. FlavaWorks notes that several members resolved the claims before they were named. Additionally, in its separate RICO lawsuit against 75 members, one John Doe agreed to pay an undisclosed settlement amount in installments.

For now, the account holders and the subpoenaed companies can still ask the court to quash the subpoenas, but the docket shows no movement on that front yet.

—

A copy of Judge Blakey’s order is available here (pdf). FlavaWorks’ renewed motion for expedited discovery, with the defendant-to-provider table, can be found here (pdf), and the September status report is available here (pdf). FlavaWorks’ July discovery motion, which mentions Google’s earlier productions, can be found here (pdf).

item.title: Streamed, the Live Sports Engine Behind Many Pirate Sites, Shuts Down
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

Live sports piracy service Streamed, which offered streams to many pirate sites, has surprisingly shut down. Its operators posted a brief farewell message without further detail, pointing visitors to five alternative sites. Earlier this month, the MPA marked the service as a growing threat in its submission to the U.S. Trade Representative.

Pirate sports streaming sites come and go, but there are a few services that have played a more central and stable role.

These “Piracy-as-a-Service” providers offer ready-made video players that other sites can embed. This allows new pirate sites to launch live sports coverage without hosting any streams themselves.

Streamed was one of these providers. The platform focused on live sports and was used as the backbone by many other sites. However, its homepage now suggests that this has come to an abrupt end.

“We are no longer operating Streamed. Thank you for the support over the years,” the message reads.

Streamed closure

The operators don’t explain why they decided to pull the plug.

Pointing to Rivals

The notice isn’t limited to streamed.pk. The strmd.link domain redirects to the closure page and streamed.st shows the same message.

Instead of simply going dark, the operators offer some advice to former users. They list five alternative sports streaming sites, each with a short description of its niche. This includes ppv.st, pitsport.st and thedaddy.pk. The latter has “lots of ads” according to the recommendation.

The shutdown of Streamed is significant as it affects dozens of sites at once. It was also seen as a notorious piracy threat by the Motion Picture Association.

The MPA previously mentioned Mapple as one of the sites that relied on Streamed. At the time of writing, some of its sports streams return a 404 error.

404


A Growing Threat

Earlier this month, the MPA listed Streamed in its annual overview of notorious piracy markets, which it sent to the U.S. Trade Representative. The movie industry group described it as a “Piracy-as-a-Service” provider that keeps growing.

Citing Similarweb data, the MPA said that around 30 pirate sites used Streamed in July, with a combined 463 million visits. A year earlier, it counted 29 sites with 134 million visits.

According to the MPA, a significant number of the sites relying on Streamed are so-called “hydra sites,” one-stop piracy portals such as HydraHD, Rivestream, StreamEX and Mapple. Cineby is listed as an example too, although it has since shut down.

“None of the sites Streamed services host live content themselves; all traffic flows through Streamed as the PaaS, which relies entirely on its own infrastructure,” the MPA writes.

MPA on Streamed

The MPA’s data covers the sites that used the Streamed embed. The streamed.pk domain itself also received 19.76 million visits in September according to Similarweb, 56% more than the month before. Nearly half of these visits came from the United States, followed by Canada and the UK.

But Why?

Streamed’s farewell message doesn’t mention any enforcement action. There is also no seizure banner and neither the MPA nor the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE) thave said anything so far.

That doesn’t rule out any external involvement, however. In its submission, the MPA took credit for the shutdowns of Cineby and AnimeFLV. These sites didn’t mention an anti-piracy action when they went down, and no group claimed it at the time.

That said, since the closure message openly promotes other pirate streaming sites, it seems unlikely that the shutdown was part of a settlement or another agreement with Hollywood.

—

We reached out to the MPA and ACE for a comment on the shutdown, but they did not respond before publication.

item.title: Accused Impostor in Private Tracker Lawsuit Faces Contempt for Withholding Passport
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

The alleged impostor behind a lawsuit against several private torrent trackers now faces a request to hold him in civil contempt. According to the defense, he missed a deadline to hand over his passport, driver’s license, and Copyright Office paperwork. Meanwhile, the defense’s proposed discovery has blanks the missing documents were meant to fill, in addition to a subpoena for his PACER IP addresses, and requests for any AI prompts.

Last year, we reported that a filmmaker named Matthew Schneider obtained a DMCA subpoena through a California federal court, seeking information from Cloudflare on several prominent private trackers.

These trackers, including PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, Karagarga, HDBits, and Beyond-HD, allegedly shared several of his works without permission.

A few months later, the same operators were sued in an Illinois federal court. That case took a turn when defense attorneys presented evidence that the plaintiff may be an impostor, and last month the person litigating as Matthew Schneider dropped the lawsuit.

That isn’t the end of it though, as Judge Andrea R. Wood kept jurisdiction over the pending sanctions request. Before any sanctions can follow, the defense wants the court to verify the identity of the plaintiff.

At a September hearing, the man said that Matthew Schneider is his legal name and that he lives in London. In response, the court requested official paperwork to back that up.

Passport, License, Copyright Application

Judge Wood had ordered the October 2 status hearing to take place by videoconference, but the plaintiff joined by phone, noting that he had technical difficulties.

At the hearing, the judge directed him to email the courtroom deputy copies of his driver’s license, his passport, and documentation of his application to the U.S. Copyright Office by October 9.

The documents would be filed under seal and shared with the parties under a protective order. However, the deadline seemingly passed without a response.

On October 14, the plaintiff asked the court if he could share a single “independently certified and apostilled” UK government photo ID instead, to be examined by the judge alone with no access for the defense.

These privacy restrictions are warranted, he argues, citing UK data protection law. Once his government ID is exposed, he adds, that can’t be undone.

“Once opposing counsel receives Plaintiff’s sensitive government-issued identification and residential information, the resulting loss of confidentiality cannot meaningfully be reversed,” the motion reads.

‘In lieu of producing both a passport and driving licence’

If the court refuses to restrict the disclosure, he asks for a temporary stay so he can seek appellate review. The motion does not mention the Copyright Office records, however, which as far as the defense knows haven’t been shared either.

‘This Is Plaintiff’s Design’

Two days later, Erin Russell, who represents Doe 1, asked Judge Wood to order the plaintiff to explain why he shouldn’t be held in civil contempt. According to the motion, he had agreed on the record to hand over the documents.

Russell isn’t asking for punishment, at least not yet. She wants a sworn statement on what was sent and when, followed by an in-person hearing.

The identity question is more than a formality. As Russell told the court in September, any sanctions award would be uncollectible unless the court first establishes who the plaintiff actually is.

In a filing last week, Doe 1 went a step further. “Plaintiff’s refusal to produce his passport and driving license hinders the discovery plan agreed to by the parties on October 2, 2026. Defendants do not know Plaintiff’s true identity,” it reads.

The plaintiff already made it clear that he will appeal if his motion is denied, which would drag this case further along. According to Doe 1’s filing, this is no accident.

“This interference with the discovery schedule is not incidental. This is Plaintiff’s design.”

Plaintiff’s design

Blanks to Fill

In last week’s filing, Doe 1 shared its proposed discovery requests and subpoenas. Doe #10, identified in its own filing as Usenet indexer omgwtfnzbs.org, submitted a similar filing. Both are incomplete, as the defense doesn’t have the identity documents.

Doe #10 had planned to tailor its requests to the passport, license, and copyright paperwork. Without them, it switched to placeholders such as “Admit that Your legal name is [insert legal name on passport].”

Placeholders

The proposed subpoenas target Google for the plaintiff’s Gmail account, the carrier of his phone number, and the mailbox provider or landlord for his Sanborn, New York address. From the latter, Doe 1 seeks billing records, payment methods, and the addresses to which his mail is “allegedly forwarded.”

Doe 1 also wants the PACER Service Center to hand over the IP addresses the plaintiff used to access the court’s website.

The defendants are also measuring their own exposure. Both Does ask for “all documents, data, and other materials” he received from the companies he subpoenaed since August 2025.

According to the filings, that includes materials Cloudflare produced in response to the California DMCA subpoena. The exhibit they cite, which the plaintiff filed in February, is currently sealed.

Previously, Doe 1’s attorney suggested that the person behind the lawsuit had been banned from the trackers and “bears ill will” over it, hinting at a retaliatory motive.

Was ‘Do Us Part’ Made With AI?

The last set of questions deals with “Do Us Part,” one of three films the plaintiff says he made in the UK. After being ordered by the court, he submitted his version of the film in September. According to his motion, the evidence “directly refuted” the claim that his film is the Canadian production.

His film was allegedly created more than 14 years ago, but the defense appears to doubt this. They ask the plaintiff to admit that the submission “was generated, in whole or in part, using GenAI.”

GenAI

They also want the original file, all raw footage, and “all prompts, outputs, project files, account records, and activity logs” for any use of AI.

All parties can still file objections to the discovery requests and they are scheduled to meet again at a video hearing on November 17. This time, the court has directed the plaintiff to test his video capabilities before it starts.

—

The plaintiff’s motion to modify the ID order is available here (pdf). Doe 1’s contempt motion is here (pdf). The proposed discovery requests from Doe 1 and Doe #10 can be found here (pdf) and here (pdf).

Judge Wood had ordered the October 2 status hearing to take place by videoconference, but the plaintiff joined by phone, noting that he had technical difficulties.

At the hearing, the judge directed him to email the courtroom deputy copies of his driver’s license, his passport, and documentation of his application to the U.S. Copyright Office by October 9.

The documents would be filed under seal and shared with the parties under a protective order. However, the deadline seemingly passed without a response.

On October 14, the plaintiff asked the court if he could share a single “independently certified and apostilled” UK government photo ID instead, to be examined by the judge alone with no access for the defense.

These privacy restrictions are warranted, he argues, citing UK data protection law. Once his government ID is exposed, he adds, that can’t be undone.

“Once opposing counsel receives Plaintiff’s sensitive government-issued identification and residential information, the resulting loss of confidentiality cannot meaningfully be reversed,” the motion reads.

‘In lieu of producing both a passport and driving licence’

If the court refuses to restrict the disclosure, he asks for a temporary stay so he can seek appellate review. The motion does not mention the Copyright Office records, however, which as far as the defense knows haven’t been shared either.

‘This Is Plaintiff’s Design’

Two days later, Erin Russell, who represents Doe 1, asked Judge Wood to order the plaintiff to explain why he shouldn’t be held in civil contempt. According to the motion, he had agreed on the record to hand over the documents.

Russell isn’t asking for punishment, at least not yet. She wants a sworn statement on what was sent and when, followed by an in-person hearing.

The identity question is more than a formality. As Russell told the court in September, any sanctions award would be uncollectible unless the court first establishes who the plaintiff actually is.

In a filing last week, Doe 1 went a step further. “Plaintiff’s refusal to produce his passport and driving license hinders the discovery plan agreed to by the parties on October 2, 2026. Defendants do not know Plaintiff’s true identity,” it reads.

The plaintiff already made it clear that he will appeal if his motion is denied, which would drag this case further along. According to Doe 1’s filing, this is no accident.

“This interference with the discovery schedule is not incidental. This is Plaintiff’s design.”

Plaintiff’s design

Blanks to Fill

In last week’s filing, Doe 1 shared its proposed discovery requests and subpoenas. Doe #10, identified in its own filing as Usenet indexer omgwtfnzbs.org, submitted a similar filing. Both are incomplete, as the defense doesn’t have the identity documents.

Doe #10 had planned to tailor its requests to the passport, license, and copyright paperwork. Without them, it switched to placeholders such as “Admit that Your legal name is [insert legal name on passport].”

Placeholders

The proposed subpoenas target Google for the plaintiff’s Gmail account, the carrier of his phone number, and the mailbox provider or landlord for his Sanborn, New York address. From the latter, Doe 1 seeks billing records, payment methods, and the addresses to which his mail is “allegedly forwarded.”

Doe 1 also wants the PACER Service Center to hand over the IP addresses the plaintiff used to access the court’s website.

The defendants are also measuring their own exposure. Both Does ask for “all documents, data, and other materials” he received from the companies he subpoenaed since August 2025.

According to the filings, that includes materials Cloudflare produced in response to the California DMCA subpoena. The exhibit they cite, which the plaintiff filed in February, is currently sealed.

Previously, Doe 1’s attorney suggested that the person behind the lawsuit had been banned from the trackers and “bears ill will” over it, hinting at a retaliatory motive.

Was ‘Do Us Part’ Made With AI?

The last set of questions deals with “Do Us Part,” one of three films the plaintiff says he made in the UK. After being ordered by the court, he submitted his version of the film in September. According to his motion, the evidence “directly refuted” the claim that his film is the Canadian production.

His film was allegedly created more than 14 years ago, but the defense appears to doubt this. They ask the plaintiff to admit that the submission “was generated, in whole or in part, using GenAI.”

GenAI

They also want the original file, all raw footage, and “all prompts, outputs, project files, account records, and activity logs” for any use of AI.

All parties can still file objections to the discovery requests and they are scheduled to meet again at a video hearing on November 17. This time, the court has directed the plaintiff to test his video capabilities before it starts.

—

The plaintiff’s motion to modify the ID order is available here (pdf). Doe 1’s contempt motion is here (pdf). The proposed discovery requests from Doe 1 and Doe #10 can be found here (pdf) and here (pdf).

item.title: Chile Blocks 1,954 Pirate TV URLs to Protect Citizens’ ‘Privacy and Personal Data’ (1954)
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > Site Blocking >

Chile's telecoms regulator Subtel reports that local ISPs blocked 1,954 pirate streaming URLs between June and October. The blocks are part of a court order obtained by Warner Bros., but Subtel presents them as a data protection measure. Meanwhile, the piracy problem persists as several of the targeted brands remain just a search away.

Early this year, a Santiago court sided with Warner Bros. in its fight against MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV, three popular Latin American pirate streaming brands.

The 19th Civil Court of Santiago ordered all variants of these services to be blocked and instructed telecoms regulator Subtel to notify the country’s Internet providers. Subtel sent these blocking orders in January, and Warner later followed up with a criminal complaint against a local IPTV operator.

This week, new info released by Subtel shows that these initial blocking measures were just the beginning, as the blocking campaign continues to expand.

According to the regulator, the ISPs GTD, DirecTV, Entel, WOM, Mundo, ClaroVTR, Netline, and Movistar have now blocked a total of 1,954 URLs linked to illegal IPTV services. These blocklist updates come in batches, which come in regularly.

URLs blocked per month

Month URLs Share
June 221
July 180
August 469
September 319
October 765
Total 1,954

The blocked domains are not limited to MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV. Subtel also lists Cuevana, Oleada TV, Stella TV, TeleLatino, PelisPlus, Cinecalidad, and Fútbol Libre, as well as their variants and mirror sites.

Subtel’s announcement came shortly after Chilean police arrested 16 people linked to the pirate IPTV services UltraIPTV and MegaIPTV, in a separate criminal investigation.

A Matter of Data Protection

Subtel’s announcement doesn’t lead with copyright. Its headline puts digital security and data protection first, and the regulator says the procedure aims to protect citizens’ privacy and personal data.

Digital safety first (translated)

Subtel warns that these unauthorized streaming platforms can collect sensitive data from users, leaving them exposed to cybercrime, data theft, and financial fraud.

“By installing these informal apps, users expose their bank passwords, personal data, and devices to hacks and scams, without any kind of support or protection,” says Undersecretary of Telecommunications Romina Garrido (translated).

“When using a pirate app or site, users hand over the key to their personal data to unknown organizations,” Garrido adds.

The data protection argument isn’t new. Warner’s own legal action argued that the pirate platforms put users’ personal data at risk, local media reported in February.

Garrido also points users to legal alternatives. “With these blocks, we break the chain of cybercrime and promote a legal offering that actually guarantees data protection and support, such as the one offered by Chile’s formal telecommunications industry,” she says.

MagisTV and Beyond

While the court order serves as the legal basis for the blocks, the original ruling only named MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV, according to reports at the time. Since then, the piracy blocklist has expanded considerably.

According to La Tercera, other pirate TV sites were added based on an interpretation of the ruling. Subtel, the Public Prosecutor’s Office, Warner, and the Alliance Against Digital Piracy then agreed on a protocol to decide which sites should be blocked.

Subtel’s monthly figures start in June, months after the regulator notified ISPs in January. The regulator didn’t explain the gap, but it’s possible that the protocol took some time to put in place.

In practice, the anti-piracy Alliance puts together the lists of URLs, IP addresses, and domains. Subtel then forwards these to the ISPs, which implement the blocks nationwide.

The order itself is quite broad. According to Emol, it covers all variants of the three brands, including any domain, subdomain, IP address, link, redirect, or mirror site that reproduces audiovisual content, wholly or partially, without authorization.

Whac-El-Topo

Despite the growing list, the blocking efforts haven’t stopped piracy. BioBioChile found that several of the targeted sites are still online.

Our own search shows that alternatives and copycats remain easy to find as well, including sites that use the popular Cuevana, Fútbol Libre, and MagisTV brands.

MagisTV search

As shown earlier, October is the busiest month so far, with 765 blocked URLs and several days still to go. That number will likely rise further as the game of whac-a-mole continues.
